story.title: Millions Experience Total Solar Eclipse Across Europe
story.summary: On Wednesday, millions gathered across Europe to witness a total solar eclipse, the first of its kind in nearly 30 years. The eclipse's path of totality passed through parts of Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain, creating a moment of awe as the moon completely obscured the sun. Many other regions, including the UK and France, experienced a partial eclipse, with over 90% of the sun covered in some areas.

explore_lenses.label: Why did Spain need special crowd plans?
explore_lenses.title: A rare event created a short, concentrated surge
explore_lenses.summary: Spain’s totality corridor crossed populous areas during peak summer travel, turning a brief astronomical event into a transport, emergency-response and wildfire-prevention challenge.

claims.text: Spain’s government said it would use special security and civil-protection plans focused on emergency management, wildfire prevention, public safety, mobility and public-service capacity because of an exceptional concentration of people.

Before the eclipse, the government cited indicators of added travel demand: 8.4% of people planning to watch intended to travel to another province, scheduled airline seats for eclipse week were up 7.9% from 2025, and August hotel bookings were up 17.8% year over year.

AP reported that Spanish authorities expected at least 500,000 additional visitors and that hotel demand rose along the totality path; it also reported that the event took place amid high summer temperatures and wildfires.

explore_lenses.label: Why was totality so brief and location-dependent?
explore_lenses.title: Only the Moon’s narrow central shadow delivers totality
explore_lenses.summary: The event was total only inside the Moon’s umbra; elsewhere viewers saw a partial eclipse. In Spain, its late-evening timing made an unobstructed western horizon especially important.

claims.text: NASA says the 2026 path of totality ran through Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, the Atlantic, Spain and a small part of Portugal, while much of Europe and other regions saw only a partial eclipse.

NASA explains that totality occurs only in the Moon’s inner shadow, or umbra; most people in the path had less than two minutes of totality, and even the longest central-path duration was under two and a half minutes.

Spain’s National Geographic Institute said the eclipse reached the country near sunset, requiring a clear view west; it projected totality ranging from 76 seconds in A Coruña to 104 seconds in Burgos, while Palma’s maximum came with the Sun only 2 degrees above the horizon.
NASA says the corona is visible during totality and that eclipse observations can help investigate how heat and energy move from the Sun into the solar wind.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after Europe’s 2026 eclipse?
explore_lenses.title: Scientists will analyze observations; Spain has another total eclipse in 2027
explore_lenses.summary: The spectacle also supported solar and atmospheric research, while Spain’s run of major eclipses continues next year.

claims.text: NASA said its 2026 campaign included a WB-57 high-altitude aircraft to study coronal dynamics and balloon launches in Iceland and Spain to examine how temporary eclipse darkness affects Earth’s atmosphere.
NASA’s research plan said the aircraft cameras would record rapid coronal structures and changes, while the balloon project would measure atmospheric effects before, during and after totality.

Spain’s National Geographic Institute lists the next total solar eclipse visible from Spain for August 2, 2027, followed by an annular eclipse on January 26, 2028; it says another total eclipse will not be visible from Spain until 2053.

story_report.summary: Millions of people gathered across Europe to watch a total solar eclipse, the first visible on the continent in nearly 30 years. Totality crossed Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain, while much of Europe saw a partial eclipse. Large crowds, particularly in Spain, brought added travel demand and prompted authorities to prepare security, mobility and civil-protection measures for an exceptional concentration of visitors.

sections.heading: Spain Prepares for Eclipse Crowds
sections.body: Spain’s government activated special plans covering emergency management, wildfire prevention, public safety, transport and public-service capacity. Before the event, it said 8.4% of prospective viewers planned to travel to another province; scheduled airline seats for eclipse week were 7.9% above 2025 levels and August hotel bookings were up 17.8% year over year. AP reported authorities expected at least 500,000 additional visitors, with demand rising along the totality path during high temperatures and wildfires.

sections.heading: Totality Offers a Brief Window
sections.body: NASA said the narrow path of totality also crossed northern Russia, the Atlantic and a small part of Portugal, while viewers outside the Moon’s inner shadow saw only a partial eclipse. Most locations in the path received less than two minutes of totality, and the longest duration on the central path was under two and a half minutes. In Spain, the eclipse arrived near sunset: projected totality ranged from 76 seconds in A Coruña to 104 seconds in Burgos, requiring a clear western horizon.

sections.heading: Eclipse Supports Solar Research
sections.body: During totality, the Sun’s corona becomes visible, offering researchers an opportunity to study how heat and energy move into the solar wind. NASA’s campaign included a WB-57 high-altitude aircraft to record rapid changes in coronal structures and balloon launches in Iceland and Spain to measure atmospheric effects before, during and after totality. Spain’s next total eclipse visible from the country is scheduled for Aug. 2, 2027; another will not be visible there until 2053.

related_stories.summary: California beaches are experiencing a surge in round stingray populations, attributed to warmer coastal waters and the anticipated effects of a strong El Niño. This increase has resulted in a record number of injuries among beachgoers as the stingrays come closer to shore.
